title: Se, Sp, PPV, and prevalence
dek: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of a test in a population. Predictive values are properties of a test in your waiting room. TB diagnostics die when people swap those.
story: Sensitivity: P(positive | disease). Specificity: P(negative | no disease). They do not know your prevalence. Positive predictive value: P(disease | positive) = Se·p / (Se·p + (1−Sp)·(1−p)). That is Bayes with a binary test, and it is why Ultra in a community survey is not Ultra in a TB ward.
LF-LAM, CAD, TST, and even Xpert acquire different PPV as p changes. Publishing “Xpert PPV 98%” without p is an incomplete sentence. So is “LAM is insensitive” without CD4 stratum.

Likelihood ratios (Se/(1−Sp) and (1−Se)/Sp) let you move log-odds without re-deriving Bayes each time. They still assume the Se/Sp you measured apply to this person — spectrum bias is how HIV and pediatric TB punish you.
deep: PPV = Se p / (Se p + FPR (1−p)), FPR = 1−Sp. NPV = Sp (1−p) / (Sp (1−p) + FNR p), FNR = 1−Se.
When p → 0, PPV → 0 even for excellent tests. That is screening. Confirmatory mWRDs exist because triage tests are not allowed to have the last word.
Heteroresistance and mixed samples break the implicit “one true disease state” in Se/Sp tables. Your residual is not always noise.
Do not average Se across smear-positive and pediatric gastric-aspirate cohorts and then quote one number to a clinician.

example.setup: Ultra Se 0.90, Sp 0.98. Clinic prevalence among tested 0.25. Community survey prevalence 0.01.

steps.title: Same cartridge
steps.body: The chemistry did not change. The waiting room did.

example.takeaway: Quote Se/Sp with p, or quote PPV with p. Never a floating 98%.
